He'd been reading tiny, unconscious movements in their faces - which makes him the cleverest one in the room, just not at math.

metadata.title: Random But True: The Horse That Fooled Scientists at Math
metadata.caption:
Clever Hans could apparently add, subtract and tell the time - tapping out answers with his hoof in front of crowds in early 1900s Germany.

A formal commission investigated in 1904 and found no trickery. His owner wasn't a con man; he believed it too.

Then in 1907 Oskar Pfungst ran the test that cracked it: he asked Hans questions where nobody in the room knew the answer. Hans failed almost every time.

The horse had been reading involuntary body language - tiny shifts the questioners had no idea they were making - and stopping his hoof when he saw them.

It's still called the Clever Hans effect, and researchers design experiments around it to this day.

Comment if you think that's more impressive than doing the math.
